title: SpaceX Starship Flight 14 Launch Time Revealed: Full Sept. 28 Orbital Test Schedule Unveiled
body:
SpaceX is set to stage the next milestone in its Starship program on September 28, when the company will attempt the first orbital flight of its Starship Flight 14 prototype from the Boca Chica launch site in Texas. The launch window opens at 2:12 a.m. Central Daylight Time (UTC‑5) and will close at 3:02 a.m., giving the launch team a 50‑minute window to clear the vehicle for liftoff. If successful, the mission will be the first to carry the fully stacked Starship system—comprising the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage—beyond Earth’s atmosphere, marking a pivotal step toward SpaceX’s long‑term vision of reusable interplanetary transport.

The upcoming test follows a series of incremental demonstrations that have gradually increased the complexity of Starship’s flight profile. Earlier in the year, the program achieved its first successful high‑altitude flight with Starship SN15, which demonstrated a controlled landing after a 10‑kilometer ascent. Subsequent static‑fire tests of the Super Heavy booster have validated the performance of the Raptor engines at full thrust, while the integrated vehicle has undergone a series of wet dress rehearsals to verify fueling, countdown, and abort procedures. Flight 14 will be the first occasion on which the entire stack is ignited and guided through the atmosphere, with the booster expected to separate after roughly two minutes before the Starship upper stage continues on a sub‑orbital trajectory before re‑entry.

Technical challenges remain, and the launch window reflects the tight constraints imposed by both the vehicle’s design and the local environment. The Super Heavy booster, standing 69 meters tall and powered by 33 Raptor engines, must generate enough thrust to overcome the weight of the fully fueled Starship, which carries roughly 1,200 tonnes of propellant. Engineers have been fine‑tuning the engine throttle profiles to manage vibration and acoustic loads that could jeopardize structural integrity. Moreover, Boca Chica’s proximity to the Gulf of Mexico imposes strict range safety requirements; the flight path is planned to avoid populated areas, with the vehicle slated to splash down in the Atlantic if the mission proceeds as intended.

Industry observers see Flight 14 as a litmus test for SpaceX’s broader ambitions, including the planned Starship missions to the Moon under NASA’s Artemis program and the eventual goal of crewed journeys to Mars. A successful orbital flight would demonstrate the system’s ability to reach orbital velocity, execute a controlled re‑entry, and perform a soft splash‑down—capabilities essential for the rapid‑turnaround, fully reusable architecture SpaceX envisions. Conversely, a failure could push back timelines for upcoming contracts and increase scrutiny from regulators who have been closely monitoring the environmental impact of repeated launches from the Texas site.

The launch also carries geopolitical and commercial significance. As rival launch providers in the United States and abroad accelerate their own heavy‑lift development, SpaceX’s progress with Starship could reshape the market for satellite deployment, deep‑space exploration, and point‑to‑point Earth transport. The company’s ability to deliver payloads at a fraction of the cost of traditional rockets could make high‑capacity missions economically viable, opening new opportunities for both government and private customers.

Looking ahead, the outcome of Flight 14 will set the cadence for the next series of test flights, each designed to incrementally expand the vehicle’s capabilities—ranging from longer orbital durations to on‑orbit refueling and eventually crewed flights. SpaceX has indicated that a successful orbital test could pave the way for a commercial launch as early as 2027, potentially ushering in a new era of space access. As the countdown approaches, the aerospace community and the public alike will be watching closely, aware that this single launch could redefine humanity’s reach beyond Earth.
